name: Victor Gupta

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: I’m with the independent Work Futures Panel. We have no ties to employers, AI companies, unions, parties or government, and we sell nothing. Your answers are confidential. What does a normal day at work look like?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I am 43, a senior developer leading accessibility software at a tech company, and I have a master’s degree. I use AI every day to draft checks, but a real screen-reader user still tells us whether a page works; I am good at fixing the hard failures. Elena runs a small tailoring shop, and we have two school-age children and a mortgage; my father’s care costs left us under one month saved despite my lower-than-usual lead pay.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d say a little AI can write repeated accessibility checks, but a user still has to tell us whether a page can be read aloud properly. I use AI daily for first drafts and test with the screen reader before release.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I lead developers and have a master’s degree, yet I earn less than most leads nearby. My wife Elena runs a small tailoring shop; after paying for my father’s care, we have under one month saved against a mortgage and two children.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d keep fixing unlabeled buttons, which a screen reader cannot name aloud, and ask our user testers about one broken page weekly. We would stop the monthly takeaway night and put 35 toward the heating bill while both incomes continue.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d feel anxious about money, not about this modest tool. My father’s care bill did not wait for our software release.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What was the last broken page?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A patient could not hear the appointment button’s name because our code left its label blank. I found the missing word in a test before the hospital put the page live.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How steady is Elena’s shop?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Wedding alterations pay well in some weeks, then nothing comes in for days. I cannot put a good month in a savings account before the mortgage takes its share.

I use **AI daily** for drafts, then check buttons aloud.
think: I earn **below lead pay** despite years of skilled work.
I have **under one month saved** after family care costs.
do: **Keep fixing** unlabeled buttons and review one user-reported page weekly.
**Stop takeaway nights** and redirect 35 monthly to heat while both incomes continue.
feel: **Anxious already** about care costs, shop income and mortgage bills.

fieldNote: His **daily AI use** serves accessibility checks that still need real user testing.
Family **care costs** and uneven tailoring orders explain thin savings despite senior skill.

steps.text: Keep fixing unlabeled buttons and reviewing weekly user reports
Stop monthly takeaway nights and reserve 35 for heating

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d say AI can write code and answer customers, but the company must not call a page accessible just because a tool ticks a box. I would ask our staff group for published job numbers and paid user testing.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Management could cut the coding team and ask fewer leads to check more sites. I think my hours or pay could shrink, and Elena’s tailoring orders would not cover the mortgage by themselves.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: This month I’d learn a new AI test for buttons whose label disappears in translation, using fake patient pages and comparing it with a screen reader. I’d bring the results and a request for paid user testers to the staff group; if my hours fall, I’d apply for paid accessibility-lead jobs elsewhere only after checking actual openings.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d be anxious, despite liking the tool. I do not want a test score to replace the person who cannot use the page.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who should be paid to test it?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: People who use screen readers every day, not just developers pretending to. I would ask the company to budget for their time before saying we have checked the problem.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Can you afford to travel for a job?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Only after an employer confirms an interview and the wage range could cover our mortgage. I would apply online first, because spare train fares do not exist in our budget.

I want **paid screen-reader users** involved in testing pages.
think: I expect **fewer leads** may have to check more websites.
I fear **my pay or hours** could shrink while Elena’s shop cannot cover the mortgage.

feel: **Anxious** about my own hours and users being overlooked.

fieldNote: He seeks **paid user testers** alongside a new AI label check.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d say full AGI by 2028 could write almost all our accessibility code and plan the tests for less. Robots for hands-on tailoring may arrive around 2031, so Elena’s sewing work changes later than my screen job.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I expect my lead job could end while we still have less than one month saved. Elena’s shop might keep selling repairs for a while, but it cannot pay the mortgage and care bills alone.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d ask our staff group now to seek written notice and paid transition terms, and Elena and I would keep the old car rather than take a new payment. If AGI arrives in 2028 and my role ends, I’d apply for paid accessibility support only where vacancies exist and wages cover our bills; I would claim any income support we qualify for during the search.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d be alarmed and wide awake at night. A clever accessibility demo does not feed two children after the pay slip stops.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell Elena?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d say her shop matters, but I will not count its best wedding week as a second full wage. We would list the mortgage and care costs before making any move.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you go into tailoring?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I can sew a button, but I am not a tailor. I might help with the shop accounts if Elena asks, yet that does not create new customers.

fieldNote: His **2028 screen-work risk** precedes robots that could reach Elena’s tailoring around 2031.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d say five years before full AGI in 2031 lets us ask real screen-reader users how a site fails, while there are still developers to fix it. Robots for tailoring may come around 2034, but my coding reaches AGI first.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I could learn more about user research and build a cash buffer if my pay improves. Yet AGI could analyse feedback too, and I will not tell my family that research is a permanent shelter.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d ask my manager for a funded three-month pilot with paid screen-reader users and take part only if the budget and my work hours are approved. I’d save 100 monthly only if a pay rise comes through and both incomes cover bills; after 2031 I’d seek paid accessibility research work only if my developer job ends and actual vacancies cover our mortgage.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d be anxious but able to test a route. A budget line and paid participants would tell me more than a hopeful meeting.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you do in the pilot?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d watch a user try to book an appointment and record each place the page stops speaking clearly. I would ask which failure cost the most time, then help turn that into a code fix.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What if the pilot is refused?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d keep my lead role and ask for paid review time on old anonymized reports. I would not claim that I had learned user research from a pilot that never started.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d say a decade before full AGI in 2036 gives us time to make accessibility checks understandable to people who use them. Robots for hands-on tailoring may arrive around 2039, after the code changes.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My children will be older, but I do not want their wages in our mortgage plan. I could build a few months saved if my employer pays me closer to a normal lead wage, though AI may still do my work in 2036.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d keep leading the accessibility team and save one anonymized example of a real screen-reader failure each month, with permission from the company. We would put 150 monthly into emergency savings only if a pay rise is approved and both incomes cover bills; if my role ends after 2036, I’d apply for paid accessibility support only where vacancies remain and the wage covers our mortgage and basic bills.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d feel anxious about the thin account today, even with ten years to prepare. I want the next care bill or house repair to be survivable without asking our children to pay it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would go into each example?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The missing label, what the user heard and the code change that fixed it, with no names. I would ask a user tester to check the wording before sharing it at work.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you leave this town?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Only for a written paid offer that covers new housing, school travel and the move. Few similar jobs are nearby, but a promise on a website is not enough to uproot us.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028 worries me most because my lead wage could disappear before we rebuild even one month of bills. Written notice, paid transition terms, eligible support and real accessibility vacancies that cover the mortgage would help; I will not count Elena’s best shop week as a full wage.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn’t ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: You did not ask who owns an AI-generated page a user cannot read. I want a named developer and a paid user tester on that decision, not a green score on a screen. A page a screen-reader user cannot read needs a named developer and a paid tester.

headlineQuote: A page a screen-reader user cannot read needs a named developer and a paid tester.
portrait: Victor is a **43-year-old senior developer** with a master’s degree, lower-than-usual lead pay and under one month saved.
He and Elena carry **two children** and a mortgage, plus his father’s care costs and variable tailoring income.
He uses **AI daily** but checks real screen-reader experiences before trusting a page.
He seeks **paid user testing** and a funded pilot, with raises required before saving more.
The **2028 case** threatens his software wage before tailoring robots may arrive later.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028** could remove his lead wage before the household rebuilds a month of savings.
whatWouldHelp: **Written notice**, paid transition terms, eligible support and bill-covering accessibility openings would help.
